cards.explanation: The answer is cousins. Abigail, Amasa's mother, and Zeruiah, Joab's mother, are sisters, so their sons are cousins. Joab is one of David's commanders, and he's the man Absalom replaced with Amasa. Cousins, and now they're on opposite sides of this fight.

The reason they give is that the people are hungry and tired and thirsty. The text says, “The people have become hungry, exhausted, and thirsty in the wilderness.” So out comes the full spread: beds, basins, earthen vessels, wheat, barley, flour, roasted grain, beans, lentils, honey, curds, sheep and cheese. That's a lot of cargo for three men, friends.

David tells his troops he will march out with them. His words are, “I will surely march out with you as well.” He says it right after splitting them under three commanders: Joab, Abishai and Ittai. So the king says he'll go in with them. Hold that thought, friends, because his people have something to say about it.

The people don't want him out there because he is worth ten thousand of them. They tell him, “But you are worth ten thousand of us.” They say that if they have to flee, or even if half of them die, the enemy will not care about them. So they ask him to support them from the city. Ten thousand to one is a number nobody can argue with.

The answer is True. David answers, “I will do whatever seems best to you…” Then he stands beside the gate while the troops march out by hundreds and by thousands. So he stays back, just as his people pleaded.

The word is gently. David commands, “Treat the young man Absalom gently for my sake.” That's his one order to Joab, Abishai and Ittai about his son. I think a father's heart is in that sentence, friends. And he says it's for his sake.

The answer is False. The whole crowd heard it. The text says, “…all the people heard the king’s orders to each of the commanders regarding Absalom.” Joab, Abishai and Ittai weren't the only ones. Remember that, friends, when a soldier says, “…we heard the king command you…” a little later.

The answer is the forest of Ephraim. That's where David's army marches to engage Israel. Keep an eye on those trees, friends, because they matter in this story. The text says that day the forest devoured more people than the sword.

The answer is True. The people of Israel, Absalom's side, are defeated by David's servants in the forest of Ephraim. The text says the slaughter is great that day, twenty thousand men. I think this is a heavy part of the story. Take a breath, friends.

The answer is head. Absalom is riding his mule when it goes under the thick branches of a large oak, and his head is caught fast in the tree. The mule keeps going, so he is suspended in midair. That's the whole reason one of David's men has something to report.

Joab answers with a question. First he says, “You just saw him!” Then he asks why the man didn't strike Absalom to the ground right there. He adds that he would have given the man ten shekels of silver and a warrior's belt.

The answer is False. The man says no, even at a thousand. His words: “Even if a thousand shekels of silver were weighed out into my hands, I would not raise my hand against the son of the king.” Joab offered ten shekels and a belt. A hundred times the silver, same answer, friends.

The answer is False. The man says that if he had jeopardized his own life, “…you would have abandoned me.” So no, he doesn't think Joab would have stood by him. He also says he wouldn't raise his hand against the son of the king, because they heard the king's command.

The troops stop chasing Absalom's army. After the ram's horn, “…the troops broke off their pursuit of Israel because Joab had restrained them.” So the chasing stops. The text says Joab is the one who held them back.

They throw him in a pit under stones. They take Absalom, cast him into a large pit in the forest, and pile a huge mound of stones over him. I think this is a quiet, sad ending to a loud life, friends. It's a heavy part of the story.

The answer is that they flee, each to his own home. All the Israelites fled, each to his home. The people who followed Absalom scatter and head back where they came from. The text says this happens meanwhile, as Absalom is cast into a large pit in the forest.

The answer is son. Absalom said, “I have no son to preserve the memory of my name.” So he gave the pillar his name, and to this day it's called Absalom's Monument. I think that's a lonely thing to say.
